strengths: Provides an interesting and relatively underexplored perspective connecting gated linear units (GLUs) to frequency-domain behavior in neural network training, motivated by the convolution theorem and differential properties of the Fourier transform.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple backbones (ResNet18, MobileNetV2, EfficientFormer-v2) and multiple frequency thresholds, showing a consistent qualitative pattern that GLUs with non-smooth activations (ReLU6) improve high-frequency classification while smooth activations (GELU) favor low-frequency components.

The proposed lightweight model GmNet achieves a competitive accuracy-latency trade-off on ImageNet-1K compared to many recent efficient architectures (RepViT, StarNet, MobileOne, EfficientFormer variants), without relying on re-parameterization or knowledge distillation.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies on GLU variants (LN, DW, pooling-based) and activation function choices, connecting the design choices back to the frequency analysis framework.
Additional bandwidth analysis of learned convolution kernels offers a complementary, if informal, piece of evidence supporting the frequency-domain narrative.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contributions (Theorem 1: convolution theorem; Theorem 2/Lemma 3: differentiability-decay relationship for Fourier transforms) are standard, well-known mathematical facts rather than novel results specific to this work; the paper largely restates textbook signal-processing theory rather than deriving new theoretical insight into gating mechanisms per se.

The connection between the abstract theoretical statements (e.g., self-convolution broadens frequency support) and the concrete claims about deep, multi-layer, nonlinear networks trained on real images is asserted rather than rigorously established; no formal analysis bridges the simple 1D theoretical setting to the actual multi-channel, multi-layer GmNet architecture.

The frequency-band classification methodology (accuracy on low-/high-pass filtered images) is adopted from prior work ([11]) without deeper methodological scrutiny of confounds (e.g., filtering artifacts, loss of semantic content at high thresholds could trivially reduce accuracy regardless of gating).

Overall novelty of the proposed architecture is limited: GmNet is essentially a lightweight block with an added simple GLU (σ(x)·x) plus depthwise convolutions, which is an incremental architectural combination rather than a fundamentally new design; the frequency framing motivates but does not uniquely necessitate this specific architecture.

Fairness of the SOTA comparison in Table 2 is not fully clear — baseline methods may have been trained with different data augmentation/regularization recipes, and the paper does not verify that all baselines are trained under identical conditions (300 epochs, same optimizer, same augmentations); this could bias the accuracy-latency comparison.

No standard deviation or confidence intervals are reported for the main ImageNet comparison table (Table 2) despite variance being reported for the smaller-scale frequency experiments (Fig. 3, Table 3), weakening statistical confidence in headline accuracy numbers.

Manuscript has notable clarity and proofreading issues: incomplete/garbled sentences (e.g., ablation description cut off with 'range/'), inconsistent terminology ('modals' instead of 'models', 'continues' instead of 'continuous', 'interact' instead of 'interaction'), which detract from readability and suggest insufficient polishing.

Key evaluations beyond ImageNet classification (object detection, segmentation) are deferred entirely to supplementary material, limiting the strength of generality claims for GmNet in the main paper.

The bandwidth analysis of convolution kernels (Fig. 7) lacks a precise definition/description of how 'bandwidth' is computed in the main text, making this evidence difficult to independently verify or reproduce.

The paper's Limitations section acknowledges that GLUs may not generalize as a universal solution for larger/more complex architectures, which somewhat undercuts the broader significance of the theoretical framework beyond the specific lightweight-model regime studied.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting question -- providing frequency-domain intuition for why gating/GLU mechanisms are effective in neural networks -- which is under-explored relative to the practical popularity of GLUs.

The proposed GmNet achieves reasonably competitive top-1 accuracy/latency trade-offs against a wide range of recent lightweight architectures on ImageNet-1K without relying on re-parameterization or distillation.

The ablation studies on different activation functions (Identity/ReLU/GELU/ReLU6) and different GLU variants (LN, DW-Conv, pooling-based) provide some empirical support for the claimed link between activation smoothness and high-/low-frequency responsiveness.

The overall qualitative narrative (element-wise product broadens spectrum; smooth activations suppress high frequencies) is a plausible and reasonably clearly presented explanation, and the paper is transparent about scope limitations for larger models.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is shallow: Theorem 1 is simply the textbook convolution theorem, and the extension to 'self-convolution broadens the spectrum, therefore NNs have more chances to learn both high and low frequencies' is a hand-wavy, non-rigorous leap -- it does not account for the fact that intermediate feature maps in trained networks are not simple band-limited signals, and the argument gives no quantitative or causal link to actual training dynamics.

Theorem 2/Lemma 3 (differentiability of a function controls the decay rate of its Fourier transform) is a well-known classical fact, not a novel technical contribution of this paper; presenting it as a 'theorem' inflates the perceived technical depth.

The link between the two theoretical results and the empirical frequency-response experiments is largely qualitative/post-hoc; no quantitative prediction derived from the theory is tested (e.g., exact predicted decay rates vs. observed spectra), so the theory functions mainly as loose motivation rather than an explanatory or predictive model.

The core architectural idea (inserting a simple σ(x)·x GLU into a DW-conv block) is incremental relative to existing lightweight designs that already use GLU-like structures (e.g., StarNet, cited and compared against in the paper itself), weakening the novelty claim of GmNet as a new architecture.

It is unclear whether baseline numbers in Table 2 were reproduced under an identical training protocol (300 epochs, same optimizer/schedule) or simply copied from original papers with different training recipes/resolutions/augmentations; this materially affects the fairness of the efficiency/accuracy comparison and is not addressed.

Frequency thresholds r used for comparing different models/architectures in Figs. 3-4 and Tables 3-5 appear to be chosen per-model ('tailored to each model' or 'to better reflect the differences') without a principled, consistent criterion, raising concerns about selective/cherry-picked presentation of frequency-band comparisons.

Despite claiming (in the checklist) that error bars/statistical significance are reported, the main results table (Table 2) shows no variance information, and the ablation tables only state 'average of five testings' without reporting standard deviation, so it is not possible to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 0.9% over RepViT-M1.0) are statistically meaningful.

Downstream task results (detection, segmentation) that would substantiate the practical benefit of capturing high-frequency information for real applications are relegated entirely to unseen supplementary material, so the paper's core practical claims cannot be fully verified from the main text.

The writing contains multiple grammatical errors and typos (e.g., 'continues' for 'continuous', 'modals' for 'models', inconsistent notation), and some claims (e.g., 'over 30% latency improvement') are stated without clear derivation, reducing overall clarity and polish expected at a top venue.

strengths: The paper offers a fresh and coherent frequency-domain lens for analyzing gating mechanisms, combining convolution-theorem-based reasoning about element-wise products with Fourier differentiation properties of activation functions, providing an intuitive explanation for why GLUs help exploit high-frequency information.

The theoretical claims are backed by consistent empirical validation across three distinct architectures (ResNet18, MobileNetV2, EfficientFormer-v2), showing that adding GLUs (especially with non-smooth activations like ReLU6) improves high-frequency component classification, which strengthens the credibility of the frequency-based narrative.

The proposed GmNet achieves a strong accuracy-latency trade-off relative to many recent lightweight baselines (StarNet, RepViT, MobileOne, EfficientFormerV2, etc.) without relying on advanced training tricks such as distillation or re-parameterization, which is a meaningful practical contribution for efficient model design.

Thorough ablation studies (activation function choice, GLU design variants, bandwidth analysis of convolution kernels) provide multiple angles of evidence supporting the core hypothesis and design choices of GmNet.
The paper explicitly discusses limitations and scope (e.g., that GLU benefits may diminish in larger/more complex architectures), showing self-awareness about the generality of the claims.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical' results (Theorem 1 on convolution theorem, Theorem 2/Lemma 3 on Fourier differentiation) are standard textbook facts rather than novel derivations; the paper's real theoretical contribution is the qualitative interpretive framework connecting these facts to gating behavior, which is more heuristic than rigorous, and the leap from these general facts to concrete architectural decisions (e.g., using ReLU6, specific kernel sizes) is not formally justified.

The frequency decomposition methodology (threshold-based radius r on 2D DFT) is somewhat coarse, and the paper does not fully justify why this particular way of splitting frequencies is the right proxy for 'information content that matters for classification,' especially given that very high-frequency components are described as 'nearly imperceptible to the human eye' yet used to draw strong conclusions.

Several quantitative claims and thresholds appear ad hoc (e.g., 'an improvement which is remarkable should exceed 1.0' in Table 5), without statistical significance testing or reported variance/error bars in the main accuracy tables (Table 2, Table 4), despite averaging over multiple runs elsewhere.

Downstream task results (detection, segmentation) that would validate the generality of the approach beyond ImageNet classification are relegated entirely to supplementary material and not discussed in the main text, weakening the significance claims made in the abstract/intro about broad applicability.

Architectural novelty is modest: GmNet is largely a conventional hybrid conv/GLU block design integrated into an existing MobileNet-style macro-architecture, and comparisons, while favorable, are against a mix of older and moderately recent baselines rather than the most current state-of-the-art efficient architectures.

Code is not released at submission time (promised only upon acceptance), limiting immediate reproducibility, and some writing/typographical issues (e.g., 'interact,' 'modals,' inconsistent phrasing) detract from overall polish.

strengths: Novel angle connecting GLU/gating mechanisms to spectral bias, linking convolution theorem (element-wise multiplication <-> frequency convolution) and activation-function smoothness (Fourier decay rate) to a network's ability to learn high-frequency information.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple backbones (ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, EfficientFormer-V2, ConvNeXt) and multiple frequency thresholds, showing a consistent pattern that non-smooth activations (ReLU/ReLU6) improve high-frequency component classification while smooth activations (GELU/SiLU) favor low-frequency components.

Strong practical results: the proposed GmNet architecture achieves a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off compared to many recent efficient models (StarNet, RepViT, EfficientFormer, MobileOne, etc.) on ImageNet-1K without relying on re-parameterization, distillation, or NAS.
Thorough ablation studies on GLU variants (LN, DW, Pool, FC-based), activation choices, and a 'contribution breakdown' table isolating the effect of the gating unit under matched FLOPs/params.

Additional supporting evidence via convolution kernel bandwidth analysis and quantitative high/low frequency energy ratios, and validation on downstream tasks (detection, instance segmentation, semantic segmentation) and a secondary dataset (CUB-100).
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is somewhat informal: the convolution theorem argument is illustrated only for idealized global self-convolution of a 1D signal and does not rigorously establish how local, learned, per-channel element-wise products embedded within a deep nonlinear network actually broaden the effective frequency spectrum of the representation. The activation-smoothness argument (Fourier decay rates) is a well-known general fact, applied here somewhat heuristically to features after several nonlinear conv layers, without a rigorous derivation connecting it to end-to-end classification accuracy.

The core diagnostic methodology (training/evaluating classifiers on radially frequency-masked images to gauge 'high/low-frequency learning ability') is a proxy metric whose relationship to a model's true internal spectral bias is not firmly established; results appear sensitive to the choice of cutoff radius r (as acknowledged in the appendix), raising concerns about robustness/cherry-picking of the reported r values in the main text.

The novelty claim of being the 'first systematic analysis of GLUs from a frequency perspective' is somewhat overstated given that the underlying Fourier facts (convolution theorem, smoothness-decay relationship, spectral bias) are all well-established in prior work; the paper's contribution is largely an application/combination of known principles rather than new theory.

Presentation and polish issues: the abstract is truncated ('Our code can be found in'), and the appendix contains artifacts suggesting rebuttal content was pasted in without proper editing (e.g., 'Following the reviewer's advice...', a broken citation '?' in Section A.7), which raises concerns about the manuscript's finalization and quality control.

Comparisons are restricted to other lightweight/efficient models; there is limited discussion of how the proposed frequency-aware gating principle would scale to larger models or interact with more advanced training recipes (though a ConvNeXt experiment is included, gains there are much smaller, which is only briefly explained).

Robustness discussion (PGD accuracy comparison) is very limited (one dataset, two activation variants, small delta), insufficient to strongly support the claimed accuracy-robustness trade-off framing highlighted as a motivating issue in the introduction.

strengths: Strong empirical results: GmNet achieves competitive/SOTA accuracy-latency trade-offs against many recent lightweight architectures (StarNet, RepViT, EfficientFormerV2, MobileOne, etc.) across four model scales on ImageNet-1K.

Extensive ablation studies in the appendix (activation function choices, GLU variants, ConvNeXt generalization, SiLU/SwiGLU comparisons, robustness under PGD, different frequency radii settings) show reasonable experimental effort.
Downstream task validation (COCO detection/instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation) suggests the architecture generalizes beyond classification.

The high-level motivation connecting gating/multiplicative interactions to spectral bias is an interesting angle that ties together several strands of prior work (spectral bias literature, GLU literature, lightweight network design).
weaknesses: The core theoretical argument is superficial: the convolution-theorem argument (self-convolution broadens the spectrum) and the smoothness/Fourier-decay argument for activations are classical 1D continuous-signal facts that are asserted to transfer directly to discrete, finite, multi-channel feature maps in CNNs without rigorous justification; broadening the frequency support does not by itself imply useful, task-relevant high-frequency information is learned rather than noise.

The frequency-component classification protocol (radially masking and separately classifying zl/zh with a model trained on full images, Fig. 1/3/4) is methodologically questionable and not well justified—these masked/reconstructed images are out-of-distribution for the classifier, so the resulting 'accuracy on zh' numbers are hard to interpret as evidence of genuine spectral bias mitigation rather than artifacts of the masking procedure.

The central architectural contribution (σ(x)·x GLU with two depth-wise convs) is a fairly incremental modification closely resembling existing GLU/Swish-style gating already used in StarNet, EfficientMod, ConvNeXt variants, etc.; the paper's claims of being 'the first systematic analysis' and offering a fundamentally new mechanism are overstated relative to the actual architectural novelty.

Several quantitative claims in the appendix (e.g., high/low frequency energy ratio Table 14, bandwidth histograms) rely on ad hoc definitions (e.g., 'low frequency = central 1/4 region') and are interpreted post-hoc to match the narrative, without statistical rigor or control experiments ruling out confounds.

Reported latency numbers for competing methods show suspicious outliers (e.g., EfficientMod-xxs at 18.2ms and EfficientMod-s at 35.3ms on mobile, versus GmNet at ~1-3ms), raising concerns about fairness/correctness of the comparison setup and undermining confidence in the efficiency claims.

Writing and manuscript polish issues suggest an incomplete/rushed submission: the abstract ends with 'Our code can be found in' with no link, the ethics statement has a missing word ('follow the ethical research standards'), a broken citation '?' appears in Appendix A.7, and Appendix A.5 explicitly references 'following the reviewer's advice,' implying content was patched in from a prior review cycle without full integration.
Single anecdotal example (Fig. 1, one 'Tiger cat' image) is used prominently to build the paper's core intuition, which is weak evidence for a general architectural principle.

Main Table 1 lacks confidence intervals/variance for the primary comparison (though some ablation tables do include ±std), making it hard to assess whether reported margins over baselines are statistically meaningful.

The comparison and interpretation versus StarNet's GLU-like design (claiming self-reinforcing vs. independent-projection gating is 'inherently more effective') is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated, relying on narrative rather than controlled theoretical or empirical isolation of this specific design difference.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and interesting lens (frequency/spectral analysis) for understanding why Gated Linear Units help lightweight networks, tying together the convolution theorem and Fourier smoothness properties of activation functions in an intuitive way.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple backbones (ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, EfficientFormer-V2, ConvNeXt) and multiple activation functions (ReLU, ReLU6, GELU, SiLU, SwiGLU), showing consistent trends that support the central hypothesis.

The proposed GmNet achieves a compelling accuracy-latency trade-off on ImageNet-1K compared to many recent efficient architectures (StarNet, RepViT, EfficientFormer, MobileOne, LSNet, etc.), without relying on re-parameterization, distillation, or NAS.

Thorough ablation studies on GLU variants (different inner operators: LN, DW-Conv, FC, pooling) and a 'contribution breakdown' table isolating the effect of gating vs. other architectural changes under matched FLOPs/params.
Good reproducibility effort: pseudo-code for blocks, detailed training hyperparameters in the appendix, and a promise to release code.

Additional validation beyond classification, including object detection/instance segmentation on COCO and semantic segmentation on ADE20K, as well as adversarial robustness (PGD) and cross-dataset (CUB-100) experiments, strengthening the generality of the claims.
weaknesses: The theoretical grounding is fairly shallow: the convolution-theorem argument (self-convolution broadens spectral support) and the smoothness-decay relationship (Fourier transform decay tied to activation smoothness) are standard textbook facts rather than a rigorous, GLU-specific theoretical contribution; the leap from generic Fourier properties to concrete predictions about GLU behavior in deep nonlinear networks is largely qualitative/hand-wavy.

The claim of being the 'first systematic analysis' of GLUs from a frequency view is a strong claim given substantial prior work on frequency bias in CNNs/transformers (Bai et al. 2022; Tang et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2020); the novelty is more in combining known ideas than in fundamentally new theory.

The core evaluation methodology of decomposing images into low-/high-frequency components and directly classifying these filtered images (which are out-of-distribution relative to natural training images) is a somewhat unconventional proxy for 'spectral bias' and its validity as a faithful measure of internal frequency usage is not rigorously justified.

Results appear sensitive to the choice of cutoff radius r (as acknowledged by additional r settings in the appendix), raising concerns about robustness/selection of the specific r=10 or r=6/12/24 settings shown in the main text.

Main comparison Table 1 (the central SOTA claim) does not report variance/error bars, unlike some ablation tables, making it harder to assess whether the reported gains over close competitors (e.g., 0.1-2% margins) are statistically robust; it is also unclear whether all baseline numbers were reproduced under identical training/latency-measurement protocols or taken directly from original papers with different settings.

The final proposed gating unit (σ(x)·x with ReLU6) is architecturally simple and closely resembles existing GLU/Swish-like designs used in prior efficient models (StarNet, EfficientMod); the primary novelty lies in activation choice and placement rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, making the architectural contribution somewhat incremental despite the added frequency-based motivation.

The paper is dense with many ad hoc empirical observations (e.g., bandwidth histograms, high/low frequency energy ratio tables) that are described narratively without strong statistical testing, which somewhat dilutes the rigor of the frequency-domain claims.
